lead: UIKit is Apple's framework of on-screen objects for iOS: views that draw and respond to touch, and view controllers that own one screen each. Interface Builder is the editor that builds a storyboard file, a saved set of screens wired to your Swift code. The wiring happens through outlets (references to views) and actions (methods a control calls). Almost every existing iOS app uses this stack, so reading a storyboard and a view controller together is a core skill.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.4 — the project must build and run before a screen can appear, and Chapter 6.3 for subclassing.

sections.h3: The UIKit layer: views and one controller per screen

blocks.text: UIKit supplies the objects that appear on an iOS screen. At the root of the tree sits UIResponder, the class that can receive touches and other events. UIView is a UIResponder that covers a rectangle and draws inside it; every label, button and text field is a UIView. UIControl is a UIView that also sends an action when the user interacts, and UIButton is a UIControl that sends its action on a tap. UILabel shows read-only text; UITextField takes typed text.

A UIViewController is not a view. It is a UIResponder that owns exactly one screen's worth of views through its view property, and it holds the code for that screen. You subclass it, one subclass per screen. The subclass adds outlets and actions; it does not do the drawing itself.
Many courses now teach SwiftUI beside or instead of storyboards.

sections.h3: A storyboard is data, loaded at run time

blocks.text: The storyboard file is data, not code. It is an XML document listing scenes, one scene per view controller, each holding an archived copy of its views and their properties. At run time UIKit unarchives a scene into real objects, allocates your view controller subclass and sets its view.

items: Object library: the list of available views you drag onto a scene.
Attributes inspector: sets a selected object's text, font, colour or placeholder, with no Swift at all.
Assistant editor: opens the Swift file beside the canvas so you can Control-drag from a view into code.

blocks.text: Every connection is stored in the storyboard as a name. Rename the outlet later, or change the action's signature, and the stored name stops matching; the app then crashes while running, not while compiling.

sections.h3: Outlets, actions and the life cycle

blocks.text: Control-dragging from a view into code creates one of two things.

An outlet is a reference to a view. @IBOutlet marks it for the storyboard. weak is correct because the view hierarchy already owns the view, so a strong outlet would add a second owner. The type is implicitly unwrapped (the !) because the outlet is nil while the controller is being created and is filled in when the scene loads. An action is a method a control calls; @IBAction exposes it to Interface Builder, and sender is the control that fired it, useful when several buttons share one action.

items: viewDidLoad — runs once, first point where outlets are guaranteed connected; one-time setup goes here.
viewWillAppear — runs before the screen is shown; repeated refresh work goes here.
viewWillDisappear — the screen is about to go away; stop timers here.

spec.aria: A phone screen with a fare label and a Show fare button; an outlet box connects to the label and an action box is called by the button, computing 8 times 11.50 and writing 92.00 into the label.

examples.question: A taxi app screen shows a label reading ₹0 and a button labelled Show fare. Tapping the button for an 8 km trip must show the fare at ₹11.50 per km. Write the outlet, the action and the placement of the code, and state the fare shown.
steps: Fare = distance × rate = 8 km × ₹11.50 per km = ₹92.00.
Declare the outlet: @IBOutlet weak var fareLabel: UILabel! — weak because the view hierarchy owns the label, implicitly unwrapped because it is nil until the scene loads.
Declare the action: @IBAction func showFare(_ sender: UIButton) — sender is the button that fired.
Inside the action work out the fare and write it: let fare = 8 * 11.50, then fareLabel.text = String(format: "₹%.2f", fare), which shows ₹92.00.
Use the outlet only after the scene has loaded: before viewDidLoad it is still nil, so any use in an initializer or an early property observer crashes.
examples.answer: The label shows ₹92.00, written by fareLabel.text = String(format: "₹%.2f", fare) when the button is tapped.
examples.check:
km = 8
rate = 11.50
fare = km * rate
print(fare)
print(km)
print(rate)

traps: Using an outlet from an initializer or a property observer that fires before loading — it is still nil and the app crashes.
Editing an @IBAction signature after connecting it; the storyboard still names the old one and the app crashes at run time, not compile time.
Believing the storyboard contains code or creates your class: it only archives objects and names connections.
Declaring an outlet strong instead of weak, which gives the view a second owner.
Confusing viewDidLoad (once, setup) with viewWillAppear (every time the screen is shown, refresh).

quiz.q: Which UIKit class does a screen's controller subclass, and how many views does it own?
quiz.a: UIViewController; it owns one screen's views through its single view property.

quiz.q: List the five view controller life-cycle methods in order.
Why is an outlet declared weak and implicitly unwrapped?
quiz.a: weak because the view hierarchy already owns the view; implicitly unwrapped because it is nil during creation and is set when the scene loads.

quiz.q: The storyboard is described as data. What does that mean for when connection errors appear?
quiz.a: Connections are stored as names in an XML file read at run time, so a broken connection crashes while running, not at compile time.

quiz.q: A text field holds a distance typed by the user and a button must show the same distance in a label. Which property of the text field do you read, and where does the code go?
quiz.a: Read the text field's text property inside the button's @IBAction; assign it to the label's text property in the same method.

quiz.q: A screen must reload a fare list every time it is shown, and also build its table once. Where does each piece of code go, and why is the other placement wrong?
quiz.a: One-time build in viewDidLoad, which runs once after outlets connect; the reload in viewWillAppear, which runs before every appearance. Putting the reload in viewDidLoad freezes the list after the first show; putting the build in viewWillAppear rebuilds it needlessly.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, storyboards are often split into one file per screen, and collection view and table view cells live in separate xib files to keep merge conflicts small. Many teams now write layout in code or move to SwiftUI, where a view is a struct and state changes redraw it. UIKit remains the base layer under SwiftUI, so outlets and view controller life cycle still appear in old code and in interview questions. Search next for "UIViewController life cycle", "storyboard reference", and "SwiftUI versus UIKit".
